Guanya Shi, an assistant professor at Carnegie Mellon University's Robotics Institute who had previously heard about OpenAl's reorganization, told Fortune that he would interpret the move as a signal that OpenAl sees robotics as "no longer a special problem." Instead, he said, they likely see robotics as a challenge that can be addressed as a downstream application of general intelligence-similar to the way the same underlying frontier Al models now power specialized coding tools, or tools for legal or financial work.
OpenAl seemed to confirm this view in its response to Fortune. It said that at the start of the year, the company's researchers assumed the best way to make progress on robotics was to build on its work on Al models such as Sora, a video generation model that, in order to create realistic videos, had to have some implicit understanding of how the physical world works.
But since then, the company spokesperson said, the company's general-purpose frontier models, including GPT-6 Astra, have shown that can be directly applied to robotics. This discovery is what motivated OpenAl to disband the stand alone robotics team and move the affiliated researchers onto teams working on more general Al models.
